utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. If you could sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness's microphones are off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And Mr. Popovic is continuing his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Before we continue, I wanted to remind you to pause briefly after I have finished putting my question, wait for the transcript, please, and then provide us with your answer so that we can help the interpreters. We will continue where we left off yesterday. We'll go back to the statement of Nike Peraj. In your binder it is tab 25. We were with paragraph number 53. Paragraph 53 where it says: "The MUP needed VJ support for large operations, and the VJ would order the MUP in large operations how to deploy and what to do." We can move on to paragraph 54 immediately the last sentence because it is related to paragraph 53, it says: "Usually, when the MUP did inform the VJ what operations it had planned, the VJ had no ability to prevent the MUP operation."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true. The army had its own chain of command, and the MUP had its own. They never interlinked. Neither could the army influence any MUP actions, nor did the army ever have a need to try and prevent any MUP actions. That is simply incorrect. Each of us had our own exclusive chain of command which we abided by throughout the NATO aggression, and we never deviated from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to paragraph 65. Here witness Peraj mentions an incident in Meja. In paragraph 65 he says: "The operation was co-ordinated from Djakovica by Lazarevic and Lieutenant-Colonel Goran Jeftovic, staff officer for operations in Pristina Corps. Could you please comment this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true. General Lazarevic on that day the 27th of April was with me, or rather I was with him at the command of the Pristina Corps in Pristina. So physically he could not have been elsewhere. As for any control of that action, as I said yesterday, it was commanded or led by Colonel Milan Kotur. He was an officer of the Pristina Corps, but he was not the commander. And he could only have been there following orders of the command or of the Chief of Staff, and he commanded from the forward command post in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that General Lazarevic was with you in Pristina, can you tell us what was the reason for that, a bit more precisely?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the national holiday of the then state which was Serbia Montenegro, the 27th of April, that is. It is for that reason that a group of officers including General Lazarevic, as well as myself, received certain decorations. There was a ceremony of awarding those decorations at the command of the Pristina Corps. After that, there was a short cocktail session and we returned to my -- and we returned to our respective units. Therefore, General Lazarevic was not in Djakovica on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am unable to follow the transcript. Thank you. Could we next move to paragraph 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: There, General, it is stated: "Close to a Serbian house in Meja, I saw three jeeps with members of the Arkan's paramilitary unit. I knew they were from his unit because I had seen them in front of our barracks in Djakovica. I recall my commander ordering me to allow access to those paramilitaries to our barracks." Can you please comment upon this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a complete untruth, as I've already said. There were no paramilitary formations in Djakovica. As for me allegedly ordering him to grant them access to our barracks, that is absurd. At that time, there was no one in our barracks because they were being constantly targeted. I could not have been in a position to direct anyone to be in any barracks because the barracks were being targeted every night. This is completely untrue and has nothing to do with reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at paragraph 83 next. There Peraj says: "Majors Zdravko Vinter who worked in the personnel department prepared a report for the staff of the 3rd Army in Nis. In the report, the VJ stated that 74 terrorists had been killed in Korenica, and 68 in Meja. On this occasion, I was able to read over Major Vinter's shoulder part of the post-operation report saying terrorists had been killed. Vinter used large fonts when typing." Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as before, I just wanted to add another thing. This was simply impossible to have happened because in the chain of command, there is a specific way of who orders whom and who reports to what person. A brigade commander cannot report to an army commander, and especially not through his subordinate officer who is even lower in terms of rank than a brigade commander. I also know where Major Vinter was at the time. This was in the cultural hall, in the cellar. It was very dark, and it would not have been possible to see what another person was typing, especially not over one's shoulder. Major Vinter had no need and had received no orders to type out any report, especially not in the command of the 3rd Army. I reject this allegation as completely unrealistic and untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next paragraph 93, please. "Milos Dosan, commander of the ARBD, theoretically speaking was the person who was supposed to command military operations in the area of Djakovica, but the operations I saw in the valley of Carragojs were ordered by General Lazarevic, Colonel Kotur, and other staff officers of the Pristina Corps. Dosan, who hailed from Bosnia and was around 48 years of age, was a sensitive person. He sympathized with those who suffered. He was not aggressive and should have been promoted to the rank of general, but his deputy after the war was promoted and received a rank senior to his own." Can you comment this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a couple of true things here. For instance, that I hail from Bosnia, that I was 48 years of age, and that I am a sensitive person. I don't see how that could be used against me. And this has no impact on my abilities as officer. I was made general, but my deputy was not Colonel Novica Stankovic, who was my establishment deputy, was never made general. Therefore, the rest is incorrect, save for the origins of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the beginning of this paragraph, it is stated that you were the person who was supposed to order military operations in the area of Djakovica. Can you comment that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the brigade commander, I had tasks, orders, and duties to command all anti-aircraft units, my anti-aircraft units. I could not have commanded over any land operations or actions. I'm not an expert in that. By profession I'm an engineer. This was far beyond my expertise, and I could not have been able to command any land actions. As I said, that action was commanded by Colonel Kotur. General Lazarevic did not command that action. And I was not supposed to and I did not command that action. That is the truth behind this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please look at paragraph 95. It says: "Dosan did not agree with the operation in Korenica and Meja and arrested Micunovic for his involvement in it. However, Micunovic remained in prison for only three days." Can you give us your comments on this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the one who plans or approves or disproves of actions. That is done by my Superior Command. So I did not approve actions or did I plan them. As for the arrest of Micunovic, I did not arrest him. I had no reason to arrest him or even any pretext to arrest him. It's not true that he was in prison for three days either. What is particularly not true is that he was released on the basis of a request made by Vojislav Seselj, Zelko Rozantovic, Arkan. Quite simply that could not have happened. Whoever was arrested was taken to the military court straightaway, and I would have known about that, so none of this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now look at paragraph 96. Witness Peraj says here: "I got authorisation to go to Ramoc from Lazarevic and Jeftovic in the headquarters in Djakovica. They passed this authorisation on to Kotur at the command post in north-east of Osek. In Lazarevic's office there was war-sized map covered in clear talc on which Jeftovic was marking details of the operation occurring in the Carragojs valley. The details I saw on the map were confirmed by what I saw when I went to the field." Can you give us your comments on this paragraph and the ability of Nike Peraj to see this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Djakovica there was the forward command post of the Pristina Corps, and he says here that that is that office. Although that is not General Lazarevic's office. He could not enter that command post. Only commanders can access command posts and only when they are asked to do so by the authorised officer involved. So he did not have an opportunity of seeing that map. Even if he had seen a map, at least half an hour is required to note details on a map, especially in infantry, to compare information from the map to information coming from the field. Nike Peraj as we have seen was a teacher by training. He did not complete the military academy. He was a traffic officer. Even if he had seen a map, he could not have made any comparisons or drawn any conclusions of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please look at paragraph 97 now, where the following is stated: "Through discussions with Stojanovic and Perovic in 1998 and early 1999, from operational briefings that I attended during the same period in Djakovica and Pristina and from operational maps that were presented in these briefings, I became aware of the general military plan for the Djakovica area. The territorial area of Djakovica municipality near the Albanian border had been divided up into three geographical areas or belts, which were to be cleared of Kosovo Albanian civilians one after the other. The villages of Meja and Korenica were included in the second belt." Can you give us your comments on this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These allegations are just the same and totally in the spirit of what has been said so far. All of these are fabrications that cannot be proven by anything and are unrealistic in their own right. Quite simply, there were no such plans. If I as brigade commander do not know about such plans, it is highly unlikely for anyone of my lower-ranking officers, especially in my own command and in my own brigade to know that. So that is absolutely not correct. Especially this is not true, that there were areas from which Albanian civilians were to be cleansed. We always struggled for the protection of these civilians, and we were not pleased at all to see columns of refugees. I did not see any one of us feeling right about seeing these columns of refugees. There were also Serbs moving to Serbia and Montenegro. When people leave their hearth, that's a very sad thing. My father left his home, and my relatives left their homes. I know what that feels like. So there certainly were no such plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I showed you some paragraphs from one of the statements given by Nike Peraj, he gave several statements, this is was the last one, and I quoted over 20 paragraphs to you, and you said that every one that I quoted to you was not true or was a lie. Can you make any assumptions as to why Nike Peraj would make such statements before this Court?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought about Nike Peraj for a long time because I received Nike Peraj at the brigade command, I talked to him, and I saw him often. When I say that, I mean that we moved very often, we were in a very small area, so we did see each other rather often. This is my observation: He carried out the tasks that I entrusted to him properly, and he properly reported on them. I think that Nike Peraj was brought into a particular situation to choose between the truth on the one hand and life on the other hand. Not only his own life but the life of his nearest and dearest. He made the logical choice. And that most people would perhaps do in his position. I don't know else I could explain that, namely that an officer makes this kind of statements. Personally, I'm convinced that quite simply he was forced into doing that and that he had no choice, either to say this or to lose someone close to him or his very own life. That's my assessment. That is what I think of him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the reason why someone would want to have him killed, and if so, who is it who would threaten him in that way?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, first of all, it would be the members of the terrorist army. He was within the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this evidence we are to accept as something of the knowledge of the witness, or is the witness trying to imagine a possible explanation? It has not been made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a witness who knows Nike Peraj personally, and he had the opportunity of spending quite a bit of time with him. He was his immediate superior. Knowing the man and knowing the situation that prevailed in Kosovo and Metohija at the time in 1998 and especially in 1999, I think -- I assumed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you are answering at length the answer shortly being this is the witness's imagination. He is trying to find an explanation. If that is the case, could you move on to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well, I'll move on to my next question. Could we please have on our screens D006-4389.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's tab 26 in your binder. Yes. General, the date of this document is the 3rd of May, 1999. It says: "Information concerning attempted rape." If you know this document, could you tell us briefly what it's about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I signed, and we are sending it on to the corps command. We are sending a report on what had happened, attempted rape, that is. It was committed by two soldiers in the area of Osek Hilja. We are informing the corps command about what we had done. Of course, the soldiers were arrested and handed over to the security organs and further on to the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00706.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'd like to see D008-0027.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Number 27 in your binder. General, we see a document of yours dated the 4th of May, 1999, that you are sending to the Pristina Corps. And you are saying where the civilian population is deployed. I'm interested in paragraph 3 that says: "The town of Djakovica has a population of 35.000 to 40.000 and there are another 20.000 to 25.000 inhabitants in villages." First of all, can you tell us on the basis of which information did you in turn send this information on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We forwarded this information on the basis of the information that we received from the municipal authorities, from the municipal government, that of course had information about the local population. Also we received information from members of the MUP. They have records of the civilian population as well. So this document is based on that. We did not do any counting. We simply base that document on that information that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your information, what was the population of Djakovica before the NATO bombing started?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the aggression started, the population of Djakovica was between 50- and 55.000. That is in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any information as to how many Serbs there were in Djakovica before the NATO aggression started?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 3.500 Serbs were there before the NATO aggression started.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: After the NATO aggression started and during the NATO aggression, do you have any information about how many Serbs left the area of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 50 per cent of the Serbs left the area of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document please be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00707.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, while we are discussing the people who left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, do you know why, what the reasons were for people leaving, especially the territory of the municipality where you were yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know because I was there all the time. There are several reasons. The first and basic reason is fear from indiscriminate persistent NATO bombing. That is the first and basic reason. And especially fear of ammunition containing depleted uranium. The next reason is fear of cross-fire because while the NATO aggression was on, terrorists were also very active and fighting against terrorists was taking place on the ground. The third reason was the persistent propaganda and fear of retaliation if they would not move out. Quite simply, the situation was such down there that a normal person could hardly take it. I am an air defence officer, and I was afraid. I can tell you that there were officers who were afraid and who fled. There were soldiers who didn't dare leave shelters. Fear is a normal phenomenon, especially for those who do not know and who cannot seek shelter or mask themselves and take other measures in order to protect themselves from air-strikes. Also, it is hard to leave first, but it is also hard to be the last person to stay. It was very hard for someone to stay if everybody was leaving. It was hard to say, I'm just going to stay on. People were afraid and that is only human. That is what I see as the reason for population movements. That is valid anywhere in the world. So that went for Serbs, Siptars. It was actually even stronger among the Siptars because it also had to do with propaganda and calls made to them. Serbs were running for their lives, the Albanians were running for their lives too from the bombing. However, they had their own guides, they had certain localities as to where they were supposed to show up, at what point in time, which routes they would take and so on. Yesterday, I talked about what happened in Meja, and I concluded that the man who was in front of them was just their guide, nothing else, and I can explain that very easily. I can explain on the basis of what I am alleging that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have D006-4401 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is your tab 29. It is your order of the 11th of May, 1999. I'm interested in item 1. It says: "Use all available measures within your jurisdiction to prevent any attempt at crime or its occurrence in the unit's combat disposition sectors. Vigorously prosecute and apply other measures against perpetrators." So May 11. Can you comment briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in no way different to other orders. We systematically monitored this persistent trend of respecting international humanitarian law and fair combat, although it is difficult to wage a war fairly against terrorists. In any case, we strove in any situation and at any level to undertake all necessary measures in order to avoid the situation in which unsoldierly conduct could serve as yet another excuse for the population to move and to leave their residence, place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00708.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I have two or three documents left that I wanted to use, and I will move through them quickly. I wanted to ask you this: Since the documents in question are maps drawn up by this witness, as such were not on the 65 ter list forwarded to the OTP, although we included them in the notification of documents we may use with this witness, if there is no objection by my learned colleague, I wanted to show those maps to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see that your learned colleague is again co-operative with your wishes, so please continue, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that. Could we please have D010-2340.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, please look at the screen since I think you will be able to see things much more clearly than in the binder and the hard copy you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D011-2340. That's the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, the title is "Deployment of the Units of the 52nd ARBR During the NATO Aggression." Are you familiar with this map? If you are, could you please tell us who created the map and what is the information contained therein?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map is familiar because I created it based on a number of documents and war diaries of my subordinate units, as well as co-operating units. We can't make things out clearly, but the map shows the positions of the units of the 52nd Air Defence Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we can see the key in the lower left-hand side corner. It says, Deployment of the 52nd ARBR before the 9th of April, and then after the 9th of April. Can you clarify why this is so?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]Yes, this is much better. Could we zoom out now so that we could see the different colours and so that the witness could explain to us what each colour means. Perhaps we could use the magic pen by Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two periods here. One is before the attempted land phase of the aggression. That is to say, before the attack on Kosare and afterwards. Before the attack on Kosare, the brigade units were concentrated mostly around the town of Djakovica in certain areas and locations from which they were able to engage air-space targets. In keeping with the envisaged tactics of the use of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What colour was used for that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really make out the colours because it is unclear as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in. I think it is yellow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so too. Yes. So mostly around Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's good. Thank you. Much better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the colour we can see. After the 9th of April and after the land phase of the aggression began, given the intended purpose of the brigade units, they were deployed throughout Kosovo and Metohija with the aim of defending certain elements of the corps command deployment. In Djakovica what was left there was the command and the logistics battalion. In the general area of Djakovica, there was the 3rd Artillery Battalion, as you can see here. This is the 3rd Battalion and the 1st Battalion was sent to the area of Kijevo. The 2nd Battalion to the area of Pristina. Am I of moving this or is someone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion was in Djakovica and Pec, the 1st Battalion in Kijevo, the 4th Battalion in the area of Pristina, and the 2nd Battalion in the area Gnjilane. Their task was to defend the air-space concerned and defend certain facilities which may be attacked in the course of the land phase of the aggression which was expected to take place. Kosare was a clear indication of the possibility of such an aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, we can see certain parts, boxes with text. What is the text about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I symbolically tried to indicate where -- the places where certain members of my unit were killed by either terrorists or NATO aircraft, as well as to indicate the locations at which NATO airplanes targeted civilians in separate incidents. I can't make everything out on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We needn't go into any further detail. It is all in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, I seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00709.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have D011-2349. It is another map.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it might again be easier for you to follow this on the screen. The title of this document is, "Locations Targeted by NATO Aviation in Kosovo and Metohija." Tell us, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I created it based on the war diaries of my units, as well as those of the co-operating units and after various analyses, we made after the NATO aggression was ended. This is what we tried to indicate on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on the bottom part of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the key as well as civilian losses due to NATO targeting in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What does the key say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Place of attack, attack on a column, use of depleted uranium, as well as attacks per units and areas in Kosovo by month. Had we gone into any further detail, the map would have become illegible, but we can see here clearly what locations were hit during the first month of the aggression, the second, and the third. They are indicated in different colour. For example, in red we have the period between the 24th of March and the 25th of April. In blue, between the 25th of April and the 24th of May. In yellow, between the 25th of May and the 11th of June. We also have separate indications of attacks which took place on the -- on Orthodox Christmas. This was quite illustrative of their tactics because they wouldn't let us rest even during our Christmas. This was disastrous for our combat morale and morale amongst the civilians. When we were in such a position to hear of our soldiers and civilians being killed during Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the period between the 25th of April and 24th of May was in red. It seems orange to me?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. I'm having difficulty seeing the true colours of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please leave it as it is. Again we see certain text boxes. What do those boxes contain? What kind of events?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the textural part, I specified those locations at which civilians were killed. For example, on the 3rd of May there was an attack by a NATO aircraft against a civilian bus where 17 people were killed and 44 wounded. On the 14th of April, a refugee column in Meja, which we have mentioned. Next the 1st of May, attack on a civilian bus in Lucani on an overpass where 40 civilians were killed. Among those civilians, there were parents who went to visit their sons in Kosovo and Metohija. On the 13th of May, a refugee column was attacked in Korisa on the 22nd of April, a refugee centre was attacked in Bistrazin accommodating the refugees from Republika Srpska Krajina, they were there on a cattle farm. This is all indicated in symbolic terms, but in addition to indicating the locations, we also wanted to indicate where depleted uranium was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on the bottom right-hand side corner. There is a table there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In it we have civilian losses due to NATO attacks in Kosovo and Metohija. Can you comment the table itself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have civilian losses indicated here, but only when such events occurred in groups and where there was a number of casualties in a single location. This does not indicate individual buildings being targeted when individuals were killed or if a single vehicle was attacked. And we know that occasionally they even targeted individual passenger vehicles on the move. This only indicates the more important events which in a way attracted some media attention and that were reported about and whereby the explanation offered was that it was all collateral damage. For example, Aleksinac, Surdulica and others were attacked as well, but that was in Serbia proper. This table only shows the figures in Kosovo itself. In total, 320 civilians were killed there in only these few individual actions by NATO aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go back to the central part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I see certain triangles here. What were they used for? Can you also tell us what were the usual targets of NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of the triangles indicates a single air attack. An attack could mean a single bomb or a single missile or 20 missiles or 20 bombs or 300 pieces of ammunition with depleted uranium. So an attack as such, this does not indicate hits or type of ammo because that would have been very difficult to count. All this happens at high velocity from great heights. This merely indicates the number of individual attacks. We can see here that all the attacks were mainly concentrated around populated areas, such as Pristina, which was in the lead. Next Prizren, and Djakovica. To some extent it was also Gnjilane and Urosevac. But this axis from Srbica via Pristina down to Kacanik, and the other prong between Istok, Klina, Djakovica, and Prizren all the way down to Albania. These were the two prongs of their attacks. They were basically directing people towards Albania or Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00710.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the last document D006-4412.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, that is tab 34 in your binder. I would not dwell on this one for a long time as it is about the NATO attack in zone 2 of the 549th Motorised Brigade. Can you just tell me if you are familiar with this document, who drew it up, and on the basis of what information?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a document that talks about who attacked and with how many projectiles on Djakovica and the environs. As the 2nd Motorised Battalion had its own defence zone in that area, this is a document which was drawn up only on the basis of the war diary of the commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion. And it depicts the kinds of ordnance used, what was dropped where in his defence zone. The time is not depicted here, but the ordnance is, so we can see rockets, bombs, cluster bombs, then there are flash bombs which were dropped in the Kosare region. Then also ammunition with depleted uranium. Then we also have one marking for attacks on the refugee column, and also attacks on the refugee settlement. That was his zone of responsibility as the infantry units do have a zone of responsibility by contrast to anti-aircraft units.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00711.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, did you ever hear during 1998 or 1999, that there was a plan or agreement in the Yugoslav Army to expel the Albanian population from the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that I never heard about such a plan from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: During 1998 or 1999, did you ever see or hear that there was a plan or an agreement within the Yugoslav Army to change the ethnic composition of the population in Kosovo by expelling the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just like in the answer to my previous question, I never heard or saw that there was such a plan from anyone, nor did I implement any sort of plan, nor did I do any such thing, nor did I receive any orders that might support such a plan. So I energetically refute any possibility that I was ever aware of the existence of any kind of plan aimed at changing the ethnic composition of the population of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you attending meetings as the garrison commander and met up with civilian authorities and the MUP organs, did you ever hear or see or discuss any kind of plan to expel the Kosovo Albanians and change the ethnic composition of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Not at a single meeting. I have said what we discussed at these meetings and that was the sole reason for us to meet when that was possible considering the dangers both from the enemy, from the air-space, and also the Siptar terrorist forces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, thank you. I hereby end my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yesterday during the course of your testimony you told us that from mid-1998 to the end of 1999, you were the commander of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade and were based in Djakovica municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the town of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you also told us that you, in your capacity as commander of this brigade, you regularly toured your units, the units of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if I understood correctly, you also had frequent or regular meetings with the senior officers of your brigade, that is with battalion commanders, company commanders?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not with all officers, but with commanding officers and organs of the command. I had meetings with organs of the command on a daily basis and with the commanding officers as necessary. Considering that certain artillery battalions and their commanders were deployed very far away, for example, in Gnjilane or in Pristina or Kijevo, wherever an artillery battalion was deployed, its commander was also there. That was why I had regular meetings with command organs and occasionally, and mostly while I was touring the units, I would talk with the commanders of these units and the officers who were in charge of the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where did these daily meetings that you had with commanding officers take place?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the beginning of the NATO aggression, we held the meetings at the commander's office in the Metohija barracks or in the Devet Jugovica barracks. My unit was deployed into these two barracks in Djakovica town. Most often they were held at the Metohija barracks where my command was located. After the beginning of the NATO aggression, we kept moving from one location to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So after the beginning of the NATO campaign, your command post moved from different -- or was based in different locations, you moved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you also told us that your direct superior, while you held this position of brigade commander, was General Lazarevic, the Pristina Corps Commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first period it was General Pavkovic. And then beginning, I think, at the new year or since the end of 1998, it was General Vladimir Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. And the main command post of the Pristina Corps, was in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same as with the brigade. Until the beginning of the aggression, it was in the building of the Pristina Corps Command, and then after that once the aggression began, it was also moved to various locations either within the town or in the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And as a brigade commander, did you have the duty to send regular reports to the Pristina Corps commander, be that General Pavkovic in 1998 or General Lazarevic in 1999? Was that one of your duties?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We sent daily reports but we had an advantage because a forward command post of the Pristina Corps was located in Djakovica all the time so we could bring the telegrams physically to them, but in any case, they were considered reports like any others, so the answer is yes, we did inform the command about all events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in these daily reports you would have included any activities your units were engaged in, any losses, any events that took place in which your unit participated?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for combat reports, which we sent regularly, they had their usual format. For example, under item 1, enemy activities were described. And then under item 2, activities of our forces would follow. Item 3, related to certain events such as those which you just mentioned. And finally, expenditure of ammunition and fuel would be included, and I think the last fifth item was the situation on the roads. Everything that was important for a unit to able to function normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we just focus on 1999 when General Lazarevic was commander of the Pristina Corps, in addition to sending these regular daily reports and the combat reports that you've spoken about, did you also participate in meetings or briefings with other brigade commanders and with General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened perhaps once or twice as far as I can remember at the command in Pristina. Just once or twice throughout the NATO aggression in 1999. The commanders were in different places. It was very difficult and dangerous to reach Pristina, and commanders were mainly in charge of operations. They had to carry out their basic tasks, and, as I said, it was very risky and dangerous to travel around Kosovo and Metohija, especially since the beginning of the NATO aggression, but even before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, sir. And did General Lazarevic tour his units deployed in the field, the different brigades? I'm speaking about the period in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did tour them. As a rule, a plan of a tour of units is made or it could be by the commander's personal decision. He was doing that. Just like I was touring my own units, he was also touring his subordinated units, and he was doing that very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on your interactions with General Lazarevic and the time you worked together when you held this position of brigade commander, would you say that he was commanding officer that kept himself well informed of what was going on in the ground, of events on the ground and the activities of his units? Would that be a fair assessment of General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lazarevic was a commander whom any officer would wish for his superior in every respect. It was important for him to know what the situation was like in units. It was important for him to receive reports. He tried to help us so he was a fine man and a fine commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on that answer you gave, sir, would it be fair to say if any large-scale operation had took place that involved units of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic would be aware of such an operation? He would be aware of the details of these operations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would use the word action rather than operation. Operation is a very general term. In military terminology, the word "operation" implies a huge area, numerous forces, a period of time varying between 5 to 10 days, and so on. Actions were carried out in Kosovo and Metohija, and there was only one operation being carried out and it was the operation of defence against the NATO air campaign.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction, sir. I am a layperson and I may confuse terms which for you are very clear and very distinct. Sir, just going back to my question, based on the answer you gave that General Lazarevic was a commander whom any officer would like to have as his superior in every respect, would it be fair to say, sir, that if he -- if there were any large-scale actions which involved units of the Pristina Corps Command, he would be fully informed of some -- of these actions, of the details of such actions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be informed if conditions were such that he could be informed. What do I mean by that? There were certain days on which due to the attacks of NATO aircraft all our communication systems were destroyed, and it was difficult to maintain courier service also because of this disruption of communication. But believe me, whenever it was possible for him to be informed, he demanded to be informed. However, there were situations, even in my own unit, when for as much as five days I could not get in touch with my artillery battalion deployed in Kijevo or for example in Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, I understand that, sir. You've spoken about the forward command post of the Pristina Corps, and you said that it was based throughout in Djakovica, and would I be correct to understand that you were referring to both the period of 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, both.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In 1998, General Lazarevic was Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, is it also correct that he was based almost very regularly or permanently at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica during that period, I'm talking about 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall who was the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, or who became Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps in 1999 when General Lazarevic was promoted to commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was appointed commander and promoted to the rank of general, but it doesn't matter. I remember that it was Colonel Veroljub Zivkovic who became Chief of Staff. From that moment onwards, he was in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So once Colonel Zivkovic became Chief of Staff, he was based at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the purpose of this forward command post, would it be fair to say that the purpose was to monitor closely the situation on the ground in Djakovica and especially the situation along the border area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're right. Military rules envisage that the so-called forward command post should be positioned in areas that were under the highest degree of threat. The commander should be there, the deputy commander, or an officer who they believe is professional enough to make appropriate decisions, but there has to be an authorisation for him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you refer to the commander being at the forward command post, who are you speaking of? Would this be Colonel Zivkovic, or were you speaking about someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said theoretically that it would be as follows: At a command post as soon as the commander arrives there, it automatically becomes the forward command post. However, forward command post is always placed in areas that are under the highest degree of threat, and it is usually the Chief of Staff who is there. Just like General Lazarevic was until he became corps commander. Also, Colonel Zivkovic, who later became a general too, of course, he was also in Djakovica all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And you've told us that General Lazarevic regularly toured units in the field. I take it, sir, that he would also -- if the need arose, he would also come to the forward command post in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever General Lazarevic came to tour the unit in Djakovica, he regularly went to the command post, and then we, the commanders who were closest to Djakovica would come as well. So that would be myself, the commander of the border battalion, that is to say all of those who gravitate towards that particular position. General Lazarevic never came to the command post or to Djakovica without me knowing about that. That is, after all, what military rules call for, namely that the brigade commander has to be informed of the arrival of the corps commander, although it is his right to come whenever he so wishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, sir. And once the NATO bombing campaign began in 1999, did the forward command post at Djakovica move locations in the same way that you've explained the Pristina Corps Command in Pristina moved locations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That change did take place from the barracks Devet Jugovica where it was before the aggression, the forward command post was moved according to the same system according to which I moved my command post. That is the principle involved with regard to all units, that they should be on the move all the time, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So I understand from that answer that it did not have a fixed location once the NATO campaign began in 1999? Speaking about the Djakovica forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that command post moved less frequently than, say, my command post, but it was not at a single place all the time either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yesterday during the course of your testimony you were shown the war diary of your brigade, and I don't want to go into too much detail, so I'm not going to bring it up on the screen, but do you remember, sir, discussing with my learned colleague and Mr. Popovic the war diary of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if I understood your evidence yesterday correctly, you indicated that all important events that concern your brigade were recorded in this war diary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part. For the most part. Sometimes something could have been missed but for the most part that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this would include any losses suffered but your brigade, any activities the units were engaged, attacks or any incidents that concern the units in your brigade, correct? This would be the type of information that you -- that would be included in this war diary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, just a moment ago we were talking about reporting and your reporting duties to the Pristina Corps Command. In your reports to your superiors -- or would the reports to your superiors correspond, meaning in the terms of information contained within those reports, with the information that had been included or written down in the war diary of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. Not necessarily because the form of a combat report is strictly prescribed. It is exactly stated what should be included under which paragraph. Whereas a war diary does not have a particular form. In that case --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, if I can just interrupt you there. I understand the distinction. Maybe I'll just make my question simpler. Would the reports to your superiors coincide, to a large extent with what -- I'm just speaking about the information included in the war diary, that is information about activities, events, losses suffered by the brigade, et cetera? I understand the format is completely different, we've seen examples of reports here in this court.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in most cases. Some things may have been missed, but as a rule that should be the case. However, perhaps there's something else I should add. For instance, in the war diary, the amount of ammunition or fuel spent was never recorded. Also what the situation of the roads was, things like that. That was an integral part of the combat report. However, key events in the brigade were usually recorded there. Perhaps sometimes there may have been some omissions or, well, the problem was that combat reports regularly had to be sent by 1600 hours. By 1600 hours, we had to file our combat reports. If something would happen after 1600 hours on that day, then such an event would not be included in the combat report for that day. Things are different with the war diary. The war diary wasn't sent anywhere. It was at the command all the time so every event could have been recorded in the war diary, even those that were not recorded in the combat report for that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just one final question before we take the break, just to finish with this topic. You said that if an event took place after 1600 hours, that would not go in the combat -- the daily combat report. But would that -- but it would go in the war diary. But if I understand, based on what you've told us of reporting, that it would be included in the next day's combat report, so it would be reported on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If it was of particular significance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honours, I see it's time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have the break now and resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday during the course of your evidence, you told us that in addition to being brigade commander, you were also commander of the Djakovica garrison; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you told us that during 1998 and 1999 from time to time to resolve specific matters, you would meet with the president of the municipality and the chief of the Djakovica SUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the chief of the Djakovica SUP in 1998, who he was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His last name was Adamovic in 1998. I cannot remember his first name, but I know his last name was Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would the person that you are referring to be a Mr. Dusko Adamovic; is that the person you are speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly Dusko, but know it's Adamovic, and I know that he left that position at the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when he left that position at the end of 1998, who replaced him? Do you remember the name of the person who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. He was replaced by his deputy until then, Colonel Milovan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did Colonel Kovacevic remain in the position of the chief of the Djakovica SUP throughout the period of the NATO bombing campaign?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, and this starts at transcript page 11381, you told us that in 1999 you had talks or meetings with these persons, the chief of the SUP -- the chief of the Djakovica SUP and the president of the municipality, and you said that you would meet occasionally in order to resolve specific issues. Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And on the next page, this is 11382, you said during these meetings you did not go into the subject of activities or tasks of others, they were very brief meetings, short meetings, sometimes you said even standing up, you wouldn't even sit down. Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So I understand from the evidence that you gave yesterday that you would meet with the president of the municipality and Mr. Kovacevic since we are talking about 1999, only when the need arose. These were not regular meetings, they were only occasional meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And there would be no exchange of information during these meetings about the activities that you were carrying out or that the MUP was carrying out, you wouldn't have any sort of exchange of information of the tasks each other was carrying out?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we would meet briefly and only in order to deal with the matter at hand. Not everybody would be there every time. Sometimes it was only myself and the president of the municipality. Sometimes perhaps it was the president of the municipality and Mr. Kovacevic. But we would just meet in order to resolve a particular problem. We did not go into other obligations or discussions or tasks, and we didn't have time to do so either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of the president of the municipality in 1999? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his first name was Milan or perhaps Momcilo, but his last name was Stanojevic. I think it was Momcilo Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And yesterday when you were referring to these meetings, you said the types of issues that were discussed were water-supply, power supply, those types of things, no?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us that you testified before in the Milosevic case, and I wanted to read a passage when you were put questions by Mr. Milosevic in relation to these meetings. Do you recall testifying in the Milosevic case about these meetings that you held with the SUP chiefs and the chief of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that particular question, but if that's what the transcript says, I'm sure that no one just made it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. So the passage I'm referring to starts at page 45405, and Mr. Milosevic in this passage is asking you about events in Djakovica municipality. Specifically he is asking you about a massacre on Ymer Grezda Street and which was -- had allegedly taken place on the 26th of March, 1999. And you were asked: "And you were the commander of the Djakovica garrison at the time were you not?" And you say: "Yes. I was the commander of the Djakovica garrison at the time, and I did have talks with the president of the municipality and also head of the Ministry of Interior." And later on you were asked: "When you say talks, did you have regular meetings, you were the garrison commander?" You say: "Yes." "Did you have any regular meetings with those leaders, civilian police, and other leaders at the level of Djakovica municipality?" And you said: "Yes. We did have meetings from time to time. When the need arose." "How frequent would they be?" And you say: "Well, two or three times a week depending on the situation. And therefore we exchanged information, each other's information, and at no point did I receive any information to that effect which would indicate that anything like that was going on in town or had happened in town." Do you recall giving that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that is what I said. If that is what is written there, but I believe that that is what I said. However, there's something else I would like to add. When I say "meetings," I would have an officer in my unit who was in charge of garrison affairs and that was Major Zdravko Vinter. He went to these meetings more often when it was necessary if matters in town were being dealt with. That's what I meant. But anyway, what I did say was true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, on the next page of this transcript, this is 45406, you are asked again about the same event I referred to, and Mr. Milosevic says: "Could something like that have happened without you knowing?" And you say: "No, that could not have happened. Something like that could not have happened without me knowing about it. Learning about it from the head of the municipality or from the chief of the police in Djakovica." Do you recall giving that evidence, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the chief of SUP and the president of the municipality, I did not mean them personally just like I as commander of the unit always have someone to stand in for me. I did not mean that the president of the municipality would have to call me personally or that Milan Kovacevic would have to call me personally. Rather, one of my officers would find out in the municipality or in the MUP if something like that had happened. That's what I meant. It's not that I met up with them every day or that I have occasion to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You did say, sir, that something like that could not have happened without you knowing are learning from it from the chief of the municipality or from the head of the municipality of the chief of police of Djakovica, so you are speaking about your personal knowledge that you would -- information that you would have obtained from them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think to this day. Had something like that happened, I probably would have found out. I've already said quite a few of my officers lived in Djakovica and they would hear this information and I would know about it. Once I would find out, I would notify my superiors. However, I did not receive any information about these alleged events or did I know about any such thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, but the testimony you provided in that case in relation to these meetings that you held with the SUP chief of Djakovica and the president of the municipality is quite different than the one you gave yesterday. You, in fact, said these meetings were regular, you exchanged information, and you are even suggesting that information on crimes would have been exchanged at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say an exchange of information concerning crimes, I still assert there -- there was information -- had there been information in circulation about the existence of certain crimes, I would have known about it. I would have either been told that by the municipal organs or by my officers who were in town. I have no knowledge of such crimes, and I don't think I said that I had any knowledge of those crimes back then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just asking about the evidence you gave on these meetings. Would you agree with me, sir, based on the previous testimony that we read out that these meetings, in fact, were not occasional, but that they occurred on a regular basis, sometimes two and three times a week?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not me personally with the municipal president and the chief of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But during your previous testimony, you did not make that distinction. In fact, you said that you would meet with them, you said: "Yes, we did have meetings, and we exchanged information." You were speaking about yourself attending these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I either said occasionally or I misunderstood the interpretation. May have not been sufficiently attentive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague is on his feet, but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Concerning this question, although we already have an answer, concerning the part Ms. Kravetz read out, the response was that two or three meetings were held, but never did the witness say that he attended them personally. That is why I objected to the way this question was put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That can be dealt with in re-examination if you wish. Thank you. Carry on, please, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, just to finish off with these meetings, you told us yesterday that there was no exchange of information on -- no exchange of information about each other's tasks, but you did say before that the purpose of these meetings was to exchange information, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of those meetings was not exclusively to exchange information. For example, from the chief of MUP, I received information of my soldiers for attempted rape in Crmljan I received that piece of information from him because there was a police unit there at Crmljan and a bit further afield there was a unit of mine there. These two units were separate, having separate tasks. The inhabitants complained to the police commander who was there. The chief of MUP called me and told me about it. The first piece of information I received about the attempted rape came from him. This is what I also understand as exchange of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So these meetings were not only about re-establishing water-supply, but if there was any information about crimes committed in the town, they would be discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He called me the very moment by phone when he learned about it. He did not wait until the meeting that was to be held the next day. He called me right away to tell me that my soldiers had attempted to rape two Albanian women in Crmljan. This was not a process of gathering information in order to present them at a meeting. At the moment he learned that, he called me. I got that information from him immediately given the circumstances and importance of that event because it was out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just a last question in relation to this, when you were responding to Mr. Milosevic, you said had any events as the ones he was asking you about occurred, you would have learned that from the chief of the Djakovica SUP or the head of the municipality. This was information that was exchanged between you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still believe if something like that were to take place and if people knew about it, that he would let me know. Why not? One must notify others of crimes. Whenever I learned of a crime, I took measures and informed my superiors. I do not wish to depart from that rule. I firmly believe if there is a crime, it should be made known.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you were to learn of any crimes involving MUP officers, would you inform the chief of the SUP about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to move away from this topic, sir, and take you to an exhibit that you were shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is D687. If we could have that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is a statement that you gave to the Commission For Co-operation with the ICTY. Do you recall looking at this statement yesterday, going over it with my learned colleague?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify something in relation to this statement and which I'm not sure if it was clarified yesterday, and it concerns the date. We see in the Serbian version that the date indicated that this statement was taken as the 28th of December 2002, while in the English it's shown as November. Which one is the correct date, sir? Do you recall if this was December as indicated in the Serbian when you gave this statement to the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was December, although I'm not completely certain. I see no reason why I would have put anything differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if I understand your evidence in relation to how this statement came about, you said yesterday that you were called to an interview by this commission for co-operation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said you were shown a book that was published by the Humanitarian Law Centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The Humanitarian Law Centre, sir, is that an institute or institution that's based in Belgrade and is headed by Natasha Kandic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the seat of that organisation is. Natasha Kandic does appear in our media stating that she is the director of that fund or of that centre. I didn't even know much about the Humanitarian Law Centre prior to the publishing of that book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in your statement, it indicates that this report which you've been referring to as book was called a "Kosovo As Seen, As Told."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the title of the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that you were shown portions of the book relevant to the events described here in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown that. Other commander were shown something else. They indicated certain passages from the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to understand how this statement came about, once you were shown these portions of the book, what were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me to read a certain paragraph and to write what I could recall about the specific event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in the Milosevic case when you testified about this, and this is at page 45627, you indicated also that you had the book at your house for two days and you leafed through it and read the part relating to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that this publication by the Humanitarian Law Centre was the Serbian translation of a report that had been published some years prior by the OSCE under the same name, "As Seen, As Told," or "Kosovo, As Seen, As Told?"

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I supposed as much. I supposed that it was a translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you didn't see in the cover of the report that it said OSCE human rights division?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention, but I'll take your word for it, why not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I imagine, sir, that when you read the portions of this report that related to Djakovica, you realised or noticed that the allegations contained within the report were based on statements taken from refugees that had fled Kosovo during the events that we are concerned with in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in the footnotes there were some initials. I think it said that these were statements of certain witnesses or refugees from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these would have been Kosovo Albanian refugees that it also would have been stated in the report, correct, who these persons cited in the Djakovica section were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember who these people were. It did say, though, that these were Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we just focus on the statement which is on the screen before us, I believe when you were going through this yesterday with my learned colleague you indicated that once -- I'm referring specifically to, I don't know if we have it -- yeah, we have it on the screen -- to the portion that mentions on the night when the NATO aggression started, I was at the Cabrat hill near Djakovica. And you told us yesterday you confirmed that that is where you were when the NATO bombing campaign began?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we are speaking about the night of the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The day the aggression began.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this statement yesterday, you said that from Cabrat hill you saw buildings burning in the old town of Djakovica in Katolicka Street; do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I said what I had seen, and it is the way you just read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said, sir, that you had come to the conclusion that the fire had been caused by NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to page 2 of your statement, and it's the first paragraph in the English, you say that because you were observing the firing from the hill, you could not reach any conclusions as to what had caused the fire on Katolicka Street; that is correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see it, but I could make my own conclusions because prior to that, I had heard an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you were, in fact, in a shelter that night, a shelter you were occupying up on Cabrat hill?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a shelter underground. One could hear things in it, but not see what is going on outside, not until you peek out, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to finish off that same sentence, you say, "but I assume this was the consequence of strikes by NATO planes." Now, based on what you've told us, sir, I understand this was not your personal knowledge, you didn't personally see that the fire on Katolicka Street was caused by NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I had heard an explosion and that afterwards I saw the street in flames. I supposed that the fire broke out as a result of NATO aircraft strikes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So can we agree, sir, that this was just an assumption from your part that the cause of this fire was NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed this with my subordinate officer who had seen it happen. From the shelter itself, I did not see when the bomb landed in Katolicka Street, although I heard it. And I did see Katolicka Street ablaze. But in my immediate vicinity, there was an officer who drew up a statement. I asked him what it was that he had seen. He told me that he saw NATO planes strike at the appropriate time. Based on his statement and what I could observe, I presumed that NATO air-strikes caused the burning of -- the burning down of Katolicka Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. So what you -- I mean, what you personally observed was the fire?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the fire myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you have no personal knowledge of what happened on that street?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not clear to me what you mean by personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
